extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent prosecution practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining patent applications for compliance with statutory patentability requirements (35 U.S.C. 101, 112, 102, 103), including claim construction, utility, written description, enablement, novelty, obviousness, and related procedural practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact prosecution — review all statutory requirements in initial review
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim should be reviewed for compliance with every statutory requirement for patentability in the initial review of the application, even if one or more claims are found to be deficient with respect to some statutory requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO personnel should state all reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action. Deficiencies should be explained clearly, indicate how rejections may be overcome when practicable, and show how problems may be resolved to avoid unnecessary delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine what applicant has invented and seeks to patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to focusing on statutory requirements, examiners must determine precisely what the applicant has invented and is seeking to patent, and how the claims relate to and define that invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review the complete specification (including detailed description and embodiments), the claims, and any asserted specific, substantial, and credible utilities. Correlate claim limitations to disclosure to ensure correct interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and understand any asserted utility
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO personnel should review the application to identify any asserted utility; the disclosure should indicate the practical application for the claimed invention and why the applicant believes it useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility statements must enable one of ordinary skill in the art to understand why the invention is useful. Applicant may assert more than one utility but only one is necessary; applicant may also rely on contemporaneous art to show well-established utility. See MPEP § 2107 for detailed utility guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review detailed disclosure and specific embodiments to understand the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the written description to exemplify the invention, explain how it relates to prior art, and clarify the significance of features; determine invention function and features necessary for at least one asserted practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine (A) what the invention does when used as disclosed (e.g., functionality of a programmed computer) and (B) the features necessary to accomplish at least one asserted practical application. Applicants should prepare clear disclosures to assist examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review the claims and analyze claim scope thoroughly
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims define the property rights provided by a patent and require careful scrutiny to identify boundaries of protection and how they relate to what applicant indicates is the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and evaluate each claim limitation; for processes identify steps, for products identify structures/materials. Correlate each claim limitation to all portions of the disclosure that describe it, including means/step-plus-function language. Consider the claim as a whole, not dissecting into isolated elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give claims the broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO personnel are to give claims their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the supporting disclosure (including express, implicit, or inherent disclosure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret means-plus-function limitations broadly but consistent with corresponding structures/materials and their equivalents in the specification. Use broad interpretation to reduce later overbroad claim construction; applicants may amend claims to reflect intended scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not import positive limitations from the specification into claims
rubrics_metrics.description: While the specification can determine intended meaning of terms, a positive limitation from the specification cannot be read into a claim that does not itself impose that limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim should be interpreted according to its grammar and intended meaning; only claim language limits scope unless claim is amended. See cited cases for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of language that may not be limiting in a claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain phrases often raise questions about whether they limit claim scope, such as statements of intended use or field of use, 'adapted to'/'adapted for' clauses, 'wherein' clauses, and 'whereby' clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of whether particular language is limiting depends on specific facts; these examples are not exhaustive. See MPEP §§ 2111.02 and 2111.04 and case law (e.g., Griffin v. Bertina).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the claim as a whole; avoid dissecting claimed invention into elements in isolation
rubrics_metrics.description: Every limitation in the claim must be considered together; do not evaluate elements in isolation because a new combination of known steps may be patentable even if constituents were known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Diamond v. Diehr: appropriate to treat claims as whole when assessing patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct a thorough prior art search prior to 35 U.S.C. 101 analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Before evaluating claims under 35 U.S.C. 101, examiners are expected to conduct a thorough search of prior art (both U.S. and foreign patents and nonpatent literature) to aid understanding of the invention and to inform eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search both claimed and unclaimed aspects if there is reasonable expectation those aspects may be later claimed. Include structures/materials and equivalents corresponding to means-plus-function limitations (35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph).

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 101 subject matter eligibility — two-step checks
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention must (1) fall within one of the four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter) and (2) must not be wholly directed to a judicially recognized exception (abstract ideas, laws of nature, physical phenomena).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the two-step analysis; consider preemption concerns. See MPEP § 2106 and case law (Bilski, Chakrabarty, Benson, Gottschalk). Examiners should not focus on § 101 to the detriment of 102/103/112 unless extreme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and examples of the four statutory categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Process = series of acts; Machine = concrete thing of parts/devices; Manufacture = article produced from raw materials given new forms/qualities; Composition of matter = chemical compositions and composite articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to cited case law (Cochrane v. Deener, Burr v. Duryee, Diamond v. Chakrabarty) for interpretive guidance. Business methods are not categorically excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility requirement — specific, substantial, and credible utility
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention must be useful or have utility that is specific, substantial and credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2107 for detailed utility exam guidance. Utility must be such that a person of ordinary skill understands why the applicant believes the claimed invention is useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph — three separate requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The first paragraph contains three distinct requirements: (A) adequate written description, (B) enablement, and (C) best mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate each requirement separately. See MPEP § 2163 et seq. for written description, § 2164 et seq. for enablement, and § 2165 et seq. for best mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate written description requirement (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must reasonably convey to those skilled in the art that the applicant was in possession of the claimed invention as of the date of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2163 for standards, typical circumstances that raise issues, and burden on examiner. Written description ties claim scope to disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider working examples, predictability of the art, quantity of experimentation, and evidence as a whole. Enablement must be commensurate in scope with the claims. See MPEP § 2164 et seq.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode requirement (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether, at the time of filing, the inventor possessed a best mode and whether the written description discloses the best mode sufficiently for a person skilled in the art to practice it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two-prong inquiry: inventor's possession of best mode at filing and adequacy of disclosure. Best mode deficiencies are rarely encountered in examination due to scarce supporting evidence in the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph — definiteness and identification of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Second paragraph requires that claims set forth the subject matter applicants regard as their invention and particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention (definiteness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definiteness is analyzed in light of the specification as interpreted by one of ordinary skill. If admissions indicate applicant regards the invention differently from claims, reject under § 112 second paragraph. See MPEP § 2171-§ 2172.01 and § 2173 et seq.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means/step-plus-function limitations — scope under 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: Means or step-plus-function claim limitations are interpreted to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and their equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give such limitations their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with corresponding structures in the specification and equivalents. If the disclosure is so broad that equivalents would encompass any means for performing the function, applicant may be required to demonstrate that claims are truly drawn to specific apparatus distinct from other apparatus capable of performing identical functions. See MPEP § 2181–§ 2186.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and proof regarding inherency and equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: When an examiner makes a rejection based on inherency or a prima facie case of equivalence, the burden may shift to the applicant to prove nonequivalence of a prior art element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may rebut with teachings in specification, teachings in prior art, or 37 C.F.R. 1.132 affidavit evidence. Mere allegations are insufficient; examiner should weigh indicia and require persuasive facts; see cases (In re Mulder, In re Noll, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: If nonequivalence is shown, examiner must still consider obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when applicant shows that a prior art element is not equivalent to a claimed means/step, the examiner must determine whether the claim limitation is obvious under 35 U.S.C. 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A finding of nonequivalence prevents anticipation but does not prevent a 103 rejection. The examiner may rely on multiple references or alternative grounds where prior art elements differ yet perform the claimed function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make a prima facie case before imposing a rejection; clearly communicate findings and bases
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should review all proposed rejections to confirm they can set forth a prima facie case of unpatentability; only then impose rejection in an Office action and clearly communicate findings, conclusions, and reasons supporting them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office action should present all bases for rejection. Examiners should not impose rejections without adequate factual and legal support.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102 novelty analysis — compare claimed subject matter to prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Review begins with comparison of claimed subject matter to what is known in the prior art; if no differences are found, the claimed invention lacks novelty and is to be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2131 - § 2146 for specific guidance on anticipation and prior art categories (patents, publications, public use, on sale, applications as prior art, critical reference dates, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 103 obviousness analysis — factors and prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine obviousness, assess scope/content of prior art, differences between prior art and claimed invention, and level of ordinary skill in the art to determine whether a prima facie case of obviousness exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider suggestion/motivation to modify references, reasonable expectation of success, that all claim limitations must be considered, and support rejections with rationale including implicit disclosure, scientific theory, common knowledge, or legal precedent. Consider applicant rebuttal arguments. See MPEP § 2131-§ 2146.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider secondary considerations and nonanalogous art in obviousness inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Take into account secondary considerations (e.g., commercial success, long-felt but unsolved need, failure of others) and whether prior art is nonanalogous or disparaging when evaluating obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess these objective indicia as part of the 103 analysis where appropriate; they may rebut a prima facie case of obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search scope should include unclaimed aspects reasonably likely to be claimed later
rubrics_metrics.description: A search must take into account any structure or material described in the specification and its equivalents which correspond to claimed means-plus-function limitations, and both claimed and unclaimed aspects should be searched if reasonably expected to be later claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures later claims are not allowed that the examiner could have identified earlier; search both patents and nonpatent literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overreliance on § 101 eligibility to the detriment of §§ 102, 103, 112
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 101 is a threshold test but not the sole tool for determining patentability; where a claim encompasses an abstract idea, 35 U.S.C. 112, 102, and 103 provide additional tools to ensure compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should consider all statutory requirements and not treat an application solely on § 101 grounds except in the most extreme cases.
